summary: Learners compare and order fractions with different numerators and denominators using two complementary strategies: (1) renaming both fractions to a common denominator and comparing numerators, and (2) benchmark reasoning with 0, 1/2, and 1 (deciding which side of 1/2 each fraction sits on, or whether it is near 0 or 1). Benchmarks are quick and build number sense; common denominators are general-purpose. Conclusions are justified with visual models (partitioned bars, number lines). The core misconception to guard against is whole-number bias — ordering by numerator or denominator alone. This is a known hard skill: on the 2004 NAEP, 50% of 8th-graders could not order three fractions from least to greatest.
misconceptions: Whole-number bias — ordering by numerator or denominator alone (3/8 vs 5/12 → '5 > 3 so 5/12 is bigger', or '12 > 8 so smaller') (IES)
Comparing without a common denominator (cross-adding, or comparing tops and bottoms separately)
Renaming only one fraction, or using a non-common multiple

activities.title: Strategy workbench: common denominator OR benchmark
steps: Take a pair such as 3/8 versus 5/12. Choose the common-denominator path: re-partition both bars (on paper or with a model) to the same fine grid — twenty-fourths — so 3/8 becomes 9/24 and 5/12 becomes 10/24, then compare the numerators 9 versus 10.

Take a pair such as 5/8 versus 3/7. Choose the benchmark path: place each on a number line marked 0, 1/2, 1. Decide which side of 1/2 each sits on (5/8 is more than 1/2 because 5 is more than half of 8; 3/7 is less than 1/2 because 3 is less than half of 7).
Switch into an ordering task: drag or write three or more fractions (e.g. 2/3, 3/5, 7/10) onto a line or into order, choosing whichever strategy fits the numbers.
State, for each comparison, which strategy you chose and why it suited those particular numbers.
activities.insight: Renaming two fractions to the same denominator makes them directly comparable (the comparison collapses to comparing numerators), and the 1/2 benchmark settles many comparisons at a glance without full computation. Choosing the strategy to fit the numbers is part of the skill.

activities.title: Dual-labelled and benchmark number lines
steps: Use a number line marked only 0, 1/2, 1 and place common fractions where they belong relative to those landmarks; for each, say whether it is more than, equal to, or less than one half.
Decide whether 4/9 is more or less than a half by comparing 4 with half of 9 (4.5): 4 is less than 4.5, so 4/9 < 1/2 — no common denominator needed.
Order 1/5, 4/5, 5/9 using only benchmarks: 1/5 sits just above 0, 5/9 is just over 1/2 (5 is more than 4.5), and 4/5 is near 1, giving 1/5 < 5/9 < 4/5.
For two different denominators, use a dual-labelled line (one unit sequence of marks above the line, the other below) to see where each fraction falls and which is larger.
Explain how the landmarks 0, 1/2 and 1 let you decide a comparison without finding a common denominator.
activities.insight: A number line anchored to 0, 1/2 and 1 gives fractions a magnitude and a 'side of 1/2' (and a sense of nearness to 0 or 1), so many comparisons can be read off directly; dual labelling lets two different denominators be compared on one line.

activities.title: Check and consolidate ordering and benchmark decisions
steps: Order a set such as 2/3, 3/5, 7/10 from smallest to largest and show working (e.g. common denominator 30: 3/5 = 18/30, 2/3 = 20/30, 7/10 = 21/30, giving 3/5 < 2/3 < 7/10).
Answer a quick benchmark question: 'Is 5/8 more or less than 1/2?' and justify.
Rename both fractions of a pair to a shared common denominator before comparing, and check the order you get.
Sort a set of fractions into 'less than 1/2' and 'more than 1/2'.
Keep the same-numerator shortcut in play: with equal numerators, the larger denominator gives the smaller fraction (2/3 > 2/5).
Check that a different common denominator does not change the order (e.g. using 60 instead of 30 gives the same ordering).
activities.insight: Fluent comparison means ordering correctly, choosing an efficient strategy, and justifying with a model — not just getting a final symbol right. Any valid common denominator yields the same order.

checkQuestion: Task: order these three fractions from smallest to largest and show your working — 2/3, 3/5, 7/10. Then use the benchmark 1/2 to decide quickly which is larger: 5/8 or 3/7. I'll watch which methods you use.
checkAnswer: 3/5 < 2/3 < 7/10 (common denominator 30: 3/5 = 18/30, 2/3 = 20/30, 7/10 = 21/30). And 5/8 > 3/7, because 5/8 is more than 1/2 (5 is more than half of 8) while 3/7 is less than 1/2 (3 is less than half of 7).
